title: Welcome & course overview
html:
Welcome

Effective Altruism Netherlands is a charity that builds a community of people trying to work out how to do the most good, and then doing it. We run courses like this one, support local organisers, host a co-working space in Amsterdam and organise EAGxAmsterdam.

People who have taken this course have gone on to work in government, start organisations, do research and redirect significant resources to effective causes. Some changed career. Others found ways to do more good in the job they already had.

What the course is for

The course answers one question: you have limited time and money, so how do you decide where they do the most good? Each week takes one part of it.

  • Week 1: Does it matter where you help? You meet the argument that some ways of doing good achieve far more than others, and practise showing your reasoning so that others can check it.

  • Week 2: How do we know what works? You read a charity evaluator’s cost-effectiveness estimate and build a simple one yourself.

  • Week 3: What if it can’t be measured? You estimate the value of uncertain bets, such as policy campaigns.

  • Week 4: Which problem should you work on? You compare cause areas, including global health, animal welfare and catastrophic risks.

  • Week 5: What will you do? You make a plan for your career, your giving, your political voice and helping others do more.

The weeks build on each other. In Week 5 you use all of it on your own plan and present that plan to your group.

How the course works

Each week you:

  • Read the course text and a few linked readings

  • Take a short quiz on Circle

  • Do the exercises

  • Meet your group for 75 minutes

Preparation takes about two hours most weeks. Week 5 takes longer because you write and present your plan. The first page of each week gives the breakdown.

The session is a workshop, not a seminar. You bring what you produced and help each other improve it, so do the exercises beforehand.

We built the course around practising skills and getting feedback. Research on motivation (self-determination theory) suggests people learn more, and keep going, when they feel capable, connected to others and free to reach their own conclusions.
